summary: This paper proposes SPICE-Q, a design-technology co-optimization framework for superconducting quantum processors that unifies process rules, layout, electromagnetic simulation, circuit quantization, Hamiltonian extraction, noise analysis, and manufacturing feedback into a single traceable data chain. The framework draws an analogy with classical SPICE, which transformed integrated-circuit design from trial-and-error into model-driven engineering, arguing that quantum computing requires an analogous unified infrastructure to scale from NISQ toward fault-tolerant processors.
motivation: Superconducting quantum-chip design currently relies on fragmented, isolated tools (HFSS, Qiskit Metal, pyEPR, SQcircuit, QuTiP) without unified interfaces or manufacturing feedback. Large-scale quantum processors require continuous model updating across device physics, electromagnetics, quantum dynamics, and process statistics—a capability that classical SPICE enabled for semiconductors but remains absent in quantum computing.
method: SPICE-Q organizes simulation into physical-space (EM fields, $S$-parameters, energy participation ratios) and information-space (Hamiltonians, Lindblad dynamics, decoherence) layers connected through cross-domain netlists. It implements a closed-loop design-technology co-optimization cycle: design and Monte Carlo yield prediction with process-statistical models → fabrication with standardized test structures → cryogenic measurement → Bayesian model calibration → redesign, using version-controlled model cards and parametrized cells.
result: The framework maps process deviations ($J_c$ fluctuations, capacitance variations, material loss) through device parameters ($E_J$, $E_C$) to system-level metrics (frequency distributions, coupling strength, $T_1/T_2$, yield). By explicitly incorporating manufacturing uncertainty into design optimization ($\max_x \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim p(\theta)}[\mathcal{L}(x,\theta)]$), SPICE-Q enables predictive design of manufacturable multi-qubit arrays and informs process control priorities through sensitivity analysis without requiring multiple fabrication iterations.
